claim: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide.
source: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer and the second leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide (Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sung et al., 2021

claim: Up to 50% of CRC patients develop life-threatening liver metastatic disease despite chemotherapy and targeted adjuvant therapies.
source: unfortunately, up to 50% of these patients – despite chemotherapy and targeted adjuvant therapies – often develop life-threatening liver metastatic disease in the following years (Argilés et al., 2020; Sargent et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Argilés et al., 2020 and Sargent et al., 2009

claim: Surgical resection may foster liver metastases by increasing the dissemination of CRC cells into the portal circulation.
source: it has been also proposed that this procedure may foster liver metastases by increasing the dissemination of CRC cells into the portal circulation (Chow and Chok, 2019; Denève et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chow and Chok, 2019 and Denève et al., 2013

claim: Surgical resection may enhance the adhesion of CRC cells to the liver endothelium.
source: enhancing the adhesion of CRC cells to the liver endothelium (Chambers et al., 2002; Gül et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2002 and Gül et al., 2011

claim: Surgical resection may promote transient immunosuppression awakening dormant intrahepatic micrometastases.
source: or promoting transient immunosuppression awakening dormant intrahepatic micrometastases (Ananth et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ananth et al., 2016

claim: IFNα has multiple antitumor effects including direct inhibition of cancer cell growth and angiogenesis.
source: interferon-alpha (IFNα), a pleiotropic cytokine with multiple antitumor effects such as the direct inhibition of cancer cell growth and angiogenesis (Indraccolo, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Indraccolo, 2010

claim: IFNα induces sustained upregulation of major histocompatibility complexes.
source: the sustained upregulation of major histocompatibility complexes (Gessani et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gessani et al., 2014

claim: IFNα induces innate and adaptive antitumor immune responses.
source: and the induction of innate and adaptive antitumor immune responses (Aichele et al., 2006; Curtsinger et al., 2007; Fuertes et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Aichele et al., 2006, Curtsinger et al., 2007, and Fuertes et al., 2013

claim: IFNα has a short plasma half-life of approximately 1 hour.
source: likely due to its short plasma half-life (~1 hr) (Bocci, 1994)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bocci, 1994

claim: Serum IFNα levels peaked at day 2 after MOP implantation.
source: Serum IFNα levels peaked at day 2 after MOP implantation and relative IFNα amounts (from ~100 pg/ml to ~1200 pg/ml) reflected the different MOP loading doses (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: A reduction in circulating white blood cells was detected only with the highest IFNα dose (1050 ng/day).
source: A reduction in circulating white blood cells (WBCs) but not in platelet (PLT) counts or hematocrit (HCT) was detected only with the highest dose (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: No increases in serum alanine aminotransferase (sALT) were observed at all tested IFNα doses and time points.
source: we observed no increases in serum alanine aminotransferase (sALT) at all tested doses and time points (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: The 150 ng/day IFNα dosing regimen induced a six-fold increase in Irf7 expression.
source: we observed a proportional dose response, with a six-fold increase in Irf7 expression at the 150 ng/day dosing regimen (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Continuous IFNα administration (150 ng/day for 28 days) reduces CRC metastatic growth in the liver.
source: We next tested the ability of continuous IFNα administration (150 ng/day for 28 days) to reduce CRC metastatic growth in the liver.
evidence: Supported by experimental design and subsequent results

claim: 100% of NaCl-treated mice developed multiple metastatic tumor lesions by days 21 and 28 after CRC challenge.
source: revealed that 100% of NaCl-treated mice (Figure 2E and F) develop multiple metastatic tumor lesions by days 21 and 28 after challenge
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: 45% of IFNα-treated mice challenged with MC38 cells showed absence of liver metastases throughout the entire duration of the experiment.
source: Conversely, 45% and 66% of IFNα-treated mice challenged with MC38 or CT26 cells, respectively, showed absence of liver metastases throughout the entire duration of the experiment (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: 66% of IFNα-treated mice challenged with CT26 cells showed absence of liver metastases throughout the entire duration of the experiment.
source: Conversely, 45% and 66% of IFNα-treated mice challenged with MC38 or CT26 cells, respectively, showed absence of liver metastases throughout the entire duration of the experiment (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: Approximately 33% of IFNα-treated mice challenged with MC38 cells achieved complete remission by day 50.
source: metastatic lesions eventually regressed and achieved complete remission by day 50 in approximately 33% of IFNα-treated mice that were challenged with MC38 cells and scored disease-positive at day 21 (Figure 2C and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: Continuous IFNα administration improved survival in both MC38- and CT26-challenged mice.
source: Continuous IFNα administration also improved survival, with similar rates for both MC38- and CT26-challenged mice (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H

claim: Continuous IFNα therapy does not significantly alter the growth of primary established CRC tumors.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that continuous IFNα therapy does not significantly alter the growth of primary established CRC tumors but reduces the liver metastatic potential of invasive CRC cells emerging from the cecum.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from orthotopic model

claim: Continuous IFNα therapy reduces the liver metastatic potential of invasive CRC cells emerging from the cecum.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that continuous IFNα therapy does not significantly alter the growth of primary established CRC tumors but reduces the liver metastatic potential of invasive CRC cells emerging from the cecum.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from orthotopic model

claim: The antimetastatic activity of IFNα does not require direct action on tumor cells.
source: IFNα promoted the development of a vascular antimetastatic niche characterized by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) defenestration extracellular matrix and glycocalyx deposition, thus strengthening the liver vascular barrier impairing CRC trans-sinusoidal migration, without requiring a direct action on tumor cells, hepatic stellate cells, hepatocytes, or liver dendritic cells (DCs), Kupffer cells (KCs) and liver capsular macrophages (LCMs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice

claim: The antimetastatic activity of IFNα does not require direct action on hepatic stellate cells.
source: IFNα promoted the development of a vascular antimetastatic niche characterized by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) defenestration extracellular matrix and glycocalyx deposition, thus strengthening the liver vascular barrier impairing CRC trans-sinusoidal migration, without requiring a direct action on tumor cells, hepatic stellate cells, hepatocytes, or liver dendritic cells (DCs), Kupffer cells (KCs) and liver capsular macrophages (LCMs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice

claim: The antimetastatic activity of IFNα does not require direct action on hepatocytes.
source: IFNα promoted the development of a vascular antimetastatic niche characterized by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) defenestration extracellular matrix and glycocalyx deposition, thus strengthening the liver vascular barrier impairing CRC trans-sinusoidal migration, without requiring a direct action on tumor cells, hepatic stellate cells, hepatocytes, or liver dendritic cells (DCs), Kupffer cells (KCs) and liver capsular macrophages (LCMs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice

claim: The antimetastatic activity of IFNα does not require direct action on liver dendritic cells (DCs).
source: IFNα promoted the development of a vascular antimetastatic niche characterized by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) defenestration extracellular matrix and glycocalyx deposition, thus strengthening the liver vascular barrier impairing CRC trans-sinusoidal migration, without requiring a direct action on tumor cells, hepatic stellate cells, hepatocytes, or liver dendritic cells (DCs), Kupffer cells (KCs) and liver capsular macrophages (LCMs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice

claim: The antimetastatic activity of IFNα does not require direct action on Kupffer cells (KCs).
source: IFNα promoted the development of a vascular antimetastatic niche characterized by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) defenestration extracellular matrix and glycocalyx deposition, thus strengthening the liver vascular barrier impairing CRC trans-sinusoidal migration, without requiring a direct action on tumor cells, hepatic stellate cells, hepatocytes, or liver dendritic cells (DCs), Kupffer cells (KCs) and liver capsular macrophages (LCMs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice

claim: The antimetastatic activity of IFNα does not require direct action on liver capsular macrophages (LCMs).
source: IFNα promoted the development of a vascular antimetastatic niche characterized by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs) defenestration extracellular matrix and glycocalyx deposition, thus strengthening the liver vascular barrier impairing CRC trans-sinusoidal migration, without requiring a direct action on tumor cells, hepatic stellate cells, hepatocytes, or liver dendritic cells (DCs), Kupffer cells (KCs) and liver capsular macrophages (LCMs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice

claim: Hepatic endothelial cells (HECs) mediate the anti-metastatic activity of IFNα.
source: Rather, the results identify HECs, including LSECs, as key mediators of IFNα-dependent anti-tumor activities that involve the impairment of CRC trans-sinusoidal migration and the development of long-term anti-tumor CD8+ T cell immunity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout mice

claim: Loss of Ifnar1 on hepatic endothelial cells allowed CRC lesions to grow undisturbed.
source: By contrast, the depletion of Ifnar1 on HECs allowed the lesions to grow undisturbed (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: VeCadIfnar1_KO mice treated with either NaCl or IFNα displayed very similar numbers and sizes of hepatic lesions.
source: Indeed, VeCadIfnar1_KO mice treated with either NaCl or IFNα displayed very similar numbers and sizes of hepatic lesions (Figure 4C and D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D

claim: IFNα treatment significantly decreased the frequency of sinusoidal fenestrae in Ifnar1fl/fl mice.
source: IFNα treatment of Ifnar1fl/fl mice significantly decreased the frequency of sinusoidal fenestrae and the overall porosity of LSECs (Figure 5C and D top)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C and D

claim: IFNα treatment increased the endothelial thickness in Ifnar1fl/fl mice.
source: while it increased: (i) the endothelial thickness (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: IFNα treatment increased the space of Disse density in Ifnar1fl/fl mice.
source: (ii) the space of Disse density (an indirect measure of hepatocyte microvilli density) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D; Gissen and Arias, 2015)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and citation to Gissen and Arias, 2015

claim: IFNα treatment increased the subendothelial deposition of collagen fibrils in Ifnar1fl/fl mice.
source: (iii) the subendothelial deposition of collagen fibrils (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: IFNα treatment promoted the appearance of a basal lamina in Ifnar1fl/fl mice.
source: and (iv) the appearance of a basal lamina (Figure 5D bottom and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: IFNα treatment increased the thickness of the vascular glycocalyx (GCX) in Ifnar1fl/fl mice.
source: Continuous IFNα treatment modified this network as well, increasing its thickness (Figure 5E and F top)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F

claim: IFNα treatment increased the expression of heparan sulfate (HS) in Ifnar1fl/fl mice.
source: and the expression of one of its major components, the heparan sulfate (HS) (Reitsma et al., 2007; Figure 5E and F bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and F and citation to Reitsma et al., 2007

claim: MC38GFP cells were about twofold less abundant in IFNα-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice compared to NaCl-treated controls at 24 hours after challenge.
source: Confocal IF quantification revealed that, compared to NaCl-treated Ifnar1fl/fl animals, MC38GFP cells were about ~twofold less abundant in IFNα-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice and ~threefold more abundant in VeCadIfnar1_KO mice treated with NaCl or IFNα (Figure 5A top).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Most MC38GFP cells localize intravascularly in IFNα-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice at 24 hours after challenge.
source: Moreover, confocal 3D reconstructions of liver sinusoids from IFNα-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice unveiled that by 24 hr most MC38GFP cells localize intravascularly (i.e. they did not invade the liver parenchyma)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A bottom, 5B and Figure 5—videos 1–4

claim: HECs isolated from sorted CD31+ cells contain approximately 96% of bona-fide LSECs.
source: Using SEM to assess the % of CD31+ cells bearing the typical sinusoidal fenestrae, we determined that our preparations contain ~96% of bona-fide LSECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: HECs from IFNα-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice showed 381 differentially expressed transcripts compared to NaCl-treated controls.
source: When compared to HECs isolated from NaCl-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice, HECs derived from IFNα-treated animals of the same lineage showed 381 transcripts that were differentially expressed (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A

claim: IFNα-stimulated LSECs upregulate interferon-stimulated genes including Irf7, Irf9, Mx1, Mx2, Isg15, Stat1, and Oasl1.
source: As expected, many of these up-regulated transcripts belonged to the ISG family, including Irf7, Irf9, Mx1, Mx2, Isg15, Stat1, and Oasl1 (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A and B

claim: IFNα-stimulated LSECs upregulate transcripts related to ECM/GCX organization and cell-cell/cell-matrix adhesion pathways.
source: Several transcripts related to the ECM/GCX organization or the cell-cell/cell-matrix adhesion pathways were upregulated as well (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B and D

claim: IFNα stimulation of Ifnar1-bearing HECs significantly increased MHC-I, CD86 and IL-6RA expression.
source: Following IFNα treatment, Ifnar1-bearing LSECs significantly increased MHC-I, CD86 and IL-6RA expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A

claim: IFNα-stimulated HECs from Ifnar1fl/fl mice cross-primed naïve OT-I CD8+ T cells to a similar extent as splenic DCs.
source: Once exposed to IFNα and pulsed with sOVA, HECs and sDCs from Ifnar1fl/fl mice cross-primed naïve OT-I CD8+T cells to a similar extent (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C

claim: IFNα-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice showed an increased proportion of central memory T cells (Tcm) compared to NaCl-treated controls.
source: we found that only IFNα-treated Ifnar1fl/fl mice showed an increased proportion of Tcm and decreased percentage of Tn when compared to NaCl-treated Ifnar1fl/fl controls (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: None of the Ifnar1fl/fl-cured mice showed detectable tumors after subcutaneous rechallenge with MC38 cells.
source: Notably, while the latter animals developed subcutaneous tumors that increased in size over time, none of the Ifnar1fl/fl-cured mice showed detectable lesions at any time point studied (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Continuous IFNα treatment promotes protection against secondary tumor challenge even after IFNα therapy discontinuation.
source: These results indicate that continuous IFNα treatment promotes protection against secondary tumor challenge even after IFNα therapy discontinuation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from tumor rechallenge experiments

claim: The microvascular modifications induced by IFNα were reverted after the discontinuation of IFNα therapy.
source: Notably, these microvascular modifications were reverted after the discontinuation of IFNα therapy with no impact on long-term liver functionality/viability (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-I

claim: Trans-sinusoidal migration of CRC cells is a critical limiting step in the metastatic cascade that occurs within 24 hours of CRC challenge.
source: As the process of trans-sinusoidal migration – a critical limiting step in the metastatic cascade – is known to occur within 24 hr of CRC challenge (Chambers et al., 2002; Valastyan and Weinberg, 2011; Wolf et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chambers et al., 2002, Valastyan and Weinberg, 2011, and Wolf et al., 2012

claim: LSECs in the healthy liver contain numerous fenestrae of up to 200 nm in diameter and normally lack a typical basal membrane.
source: it is noteworthy that in the 'healthy' liver, functioning as a common site for CRC metastases, LSECs contain numerous fenestrae of up to 200 nm in diameter and normally lack the typical basal membrane that characterizes the microvasculature of most other tissues and organs (Jacobs et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jacobs et al., 2010

claim: CRC patients suffering from chronic viral liver fibrotic diseases display lower incidence of hepatic metastases.
source: This fits with the evidence that CRC patients suffering from chronic viral liver fibrotic diseases characterized by hepatic endogenous type I interferon production display lower incidence of hepatic metastases (Augustin et al., 2013; Baiocchini et al., 2019; Li Destri et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Augustin et al., 2013, Baiocchini et al., 2019, and Li Destri et al., 2013

claim: Enhanced GCX deposits can act as a repulsive barrier that prevents tumor cell interactions with endothelial cells.
source: Notably, enhanced GCX deposits can act as a repulsive barrier that prevents tumor cell interactions with endothelial cells, adhesion molecules or chemokines have been previously identified as negative correlates of transendothelial migration (Glinskii et al., 2005; Mitchell and King, 2014; Offeddu et al., 2021; Wilkinson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glinskii et al., 2005, Mitchell and King, 2014, Offeddu et al., 2021, and Wilkinson et al., 2020

claim: LSEC capillarization and hepatic fibrosis are reversed when chronic liver injury resolves.
source: Additionally, both LSEC capillarization and hepatic fibrosis are reversed when chronic liver injury resolves (DeLeve, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to DeLeve, 2015

claim: IFNα treatment showed significant reduction in established fibrosis in patients with chronic viral liver diseases treated for up to 48 weeks.
source: Such notion is also supported by the absence of hepatic toxicity (Weber et al., 2015) and the significant reduction in established fibrosis in patients with chronic viral liver diseases treated with recombinant IFNα for up to 48 weeks (Li et al., 2019; Poynard et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weber et al., 2015, Li et al., 2019, and Poynard et al., 2002

claim: LSECs have efficient endocytosis capacity that is among the highest of all cell types in the body.
source: These data are consistent with the notion that IFNα-stimulated LSECs, due to their anatomical proximity and efficient endocytosis capacity that is among the highest of all cell types in the body (Sorensen and Smedsrod, 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sorensen and Smedsrod, 2020

claim: Dendritic cells releasing IFNα reduce liver metastatic colonization by CRC cells.
source: Additionally, other cell types within the hepatic niche could further amplify this IFNα-initiated cascade, as it has been shown that dendritic cells releasing IFNα also reduce liver metastatic colonization by CRC cells (Toyoshima et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Toyoshima et al., 2019

claim: CRC tumors may deregulate the Ifnar1 receptor and become refractory to IFNα therapy.
source: The notion that a minority of IFNα-treated animals develop small intrahepatic lesions that display similar proliferation, neoangiogenic and immunologic markers than untreated lesions highlights the possibility that CRC tumors, once established as macroscopic metastases, may become refractory and resistant to IFNα therapy by downregulating Ifnar1 (Boukhaled et al., 2021; Katlinski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boukhaled et al., 2021 and Katlinski et al., 2017
